nothing. What beneath this world did Hercules
leave free of conquest? Behold, all things are tamed.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text: Amid the heat what place was there for the brave man?

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
The one evil he had not yet conquered in the world,
the flame too is conquered; this also was added to the beasts:
among the labors of Hercules the fire departs.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text: Tell on, come, by what manner was the flame conquered?

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
When every band, mournful, seized upon Oeta,
the beech loses its shade for this man and lies low,
cut through at the whole trunk; this fierce man bends the pine
threatening the stars and calls it from the midst of the cloud:
about to fall, he moved the rock and bore with him
the smaller wood, as the talking oak of Chaonia once:
there stands wide a vast oak, and forbids Phoebus
and stretches its boughs beyond the whole grove;
it groans, threatening, with many a wound driven in,
and breaks the wedges, the driven steel springs back
and the iron suffers the wound and is too little rigid.
At last, when, falling and stirred, it drew its broad
ruin downward, straightway the place
let in all the rays: driven from their seats,
the birds wander, the grove cut down, the daylight
and, garrulous, with weary wings, seek their homes.
And now every tree has sounded, and the sacred
oaks too have felt the rough hand with the iron,
nor did its ancient glory profit the grove;
all the wood is heaped, and the timbers in alternate rows
lift to the stars for Hercules a narrow pyre:
the pine, to seize the flames, and the tenacious oak
and the shorter ilex. But the white poplar-wood
fills the pyre, the adornment of Hercules' brow.
But he, as a huge lion beneath the Nasamonian grove,
reclining with sick breast, bellows,
is borne along: who would believe him snatched to the flames?
His was the face of one seeking the stars, not the fires.
When he pressed upon Oeta and with his own eyes
surveyed the whole pyre, set upon it, he broke the beams.
He demanded his bow, 'Take these,' he said, 'offspring
of Poeas, these gifts, receive this gift of Alcides.
These the hydra felt, by these lie the Stymphalides
and whatever other evil I conquered from afar.
Happy in victory, young man, never in vain
will you send these against the foe; or if you wish to take
the birds from the midst of the cloud, the birds will descend
and sure of their prey the shafts will flow from heaven,
nor will this bow ever deceive your hand:
it has learned to poise the shafts and to give a sure
flight to the arrows, and the weapons, once sent
from the string, do not themselves miss their path: do you only, I beg,
furnish me the fires and the final torch.
This knot,' he said, 'which no hand has taken,
let it blaze with me through the fires; this weapon
will follow only Hercules; this too you would receive,'
he said, 'if you could bear it; let it aid your master's pyre.'
Then he asked the rigid spoils of the Nemean evil,
to be burned with him; the pyre lay hidden in the spoil.
The whole throng groaned, nor did grief remit the tears
to anyone; the mother, raging in her grief,
spread wide her eager breast, and bared down to the womb,
struck her vast breasts in great lamentation,
and beating the gods above and Jove himself with her cries,
she filled the whole place with a woman's voice.
'You make Hercules' death unsightly, mother,
restrain your tears,' he said, 'let woman's grief
go inward; why should Juno lead a joyful day
while you weep? She rejoices to behold the tears
of her rival; restrain your weak heart,
mother: it is a wrong to tear your breasts and womb,
which bore me.' And, roaring fiercely,
such as he led the hound through the Argive cities,
when, victor of Erebus, Dis scorned, he returned
while fate trembled, such he lay down upon the pyre.
Who, thus triumphing, stood joyful in the car,
a victor? What tyrant gave laws to the nations
with such a face? How great a peace his bearing wore!
Our tears clung fast, the driven grief fell
even from us ourselves; no one groaned for the man about to perish:
now it is shame to weep; she whom her sex bids
to mourn, Alcmena, clung with dry cheeks
and stood, a parent now almost like her son.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Did he send no prayers to the stars, to the gods above,
about to burn, or look to Jove in his vows?

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
He lay heedless of himself and, gazing at heaven,
sought with his eyes whether from some quarter his father
looked down upon him, then, stretching his hands, he said:
'From whatever quarter you behold your son, father,
you, you I beseech, for whom the day, joined to night,
rested as one. If both shores of Phoebus sing
my praises and the race of Scythia
and every burning land that the day scorches,
if the earth is full of peace, if no cities
groan nor anyone defiles the altars with impious rites,
if crimes are absent, admit this spirit, I beg,
into the stars; no place of infernal death
nor the mournful kingdoms of black Jove terrify me,
but to go, a shade, to those gods whom I conquered,
father, I blush. Open the day, the cloud dispelled,
that the faces of the gods may behold burning Hercules;
though you deny me the stars and the world,
you will be forced, father, against your will: if grief
shall take away any words, then open the Stygian lakes
and give me back to the fates: approve your son first:
that I may seem worthy of the stars, this day will make.
What is done is light; this day, father, will either
find a Hercules here, or condemn one.' When he had uttered this,
he demanded the flames. 'Do this, companion of Alcides,
not slothful,' he said, 'seize the Oetaean torch;
let my stepmother behold in what manner I bear the flames.
Why did your right hand tremble? Does your fearful hand
shrink from the impious crime? Give me back now the quivers,
coward, idle, unarmed—behold a hand
that might bend our bow! Why does pallor sit upon your cheeks?
Assail the torches with the spirit with which you see Alcides
lie low, wretch; look upon him about to burn.
Behold, now my father calls me and opens the poles;
I come, father.' And his face was not the same.
With trembling right hand he thrust on the burning pine.
The fire shrinks back and the torches struggle against him
and shun his limbs; but Hercules pursues
the retreating fire. You would believe Caucasus or Pindus or Athos
to burn: no sound bursts forth,
only the fire groans. O hard heart!
Typhon, set upon that pyre, monstrous,
would himself have groaned, and he who set on his shoulders
Ossa torn from the soil, fierce Enceladus;
but he, rising amid the very flames,
half-burned and torn, gazing undismayed:
'Now you are the parent of Hercules: thus to stand by the pyre,
mother,' he said, 'thus it befits the mother of Hercules.'
Set amid the heat and the threats of the flame,
unmoved, unshaken, into neither side
twisting his seized limbs, he exhorts, he warns,
he does something even as he burns; to all the attendants
he gave a brave spirit; you would think the burning man burned them.
All the throng is amazed, the flames scarce find belief,
so calm is his brow, so great the majesty in the man.
Nor does he hasten to be burned; and when now to his brave
death he had paid enough, the fire-bearing beams
he drew hither and thither, which the least flame seizes,
and turned them all into the fires, and where most
the fire overflows he seeks it again, undismayed, fierce,
then he fills his mouth with the flames: but for him
the heavy beard blazed; and when now the threatening
fire sought his face, when the flames licked his head, . . .

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Fear the fates, you gods above: so small an ash
is Hercules; to this, to this has that giant sunk!
O how great a mass, Titan, goes to nothing;
an old woman's bosom, alas for me, receives Alcides,
this is his tomb: behold, scarcely the whole urn
has Hercules filled; how light a weight to me,
on whom the whole air pressed a light weight.
To Tartarus once and the kingdoms, O son, the farthest,
about to return, you went—when from the infernal Styx
will you return again? Not that you may drag a spoil
and Theseus may again owe his light to you—
but when alone? The world, set upon you,
will hold back your shade, and will the Tartarean hound
be able to restrain you? When will you beat
the Taenarian gates? Or to what jaws shall I, your mother, be driven,
where death is entered? You go to the ghosts, to have
a single journey. Why do I waste the day with complaint?
Why, wretched life, do you endure? Why hold the light?
What Hercules can I bear again for Jove?
What son, so great, will call me, Alcmena,
his parent? O too happy, too happy,
Theban husband, you entered the regions of Tartarus
while your son flourished, and you coming the powers below
feared perhaps, because you, the father of so great a Hercules,
even though false, were there: what lands shall I, an old woman, seek,
hated by savage kings (if any savage king
is yet left)? Ah, wretched me!
Whoever, a son, groans for his slaughtered father,
will seek punishment from me, all will overwhelm me:
if some lesser Busiris or some lesser
Antaeus terrifies the world of the burning tract,
I shall be led as prey; if any avenges the herd
of the bloody Thracian, the dire herds will tear
my limbs; perhaps angry Juno
will seek punishment: hither all her grief will turn;
free at last from the conquered Alcides, untroubled,
I survive, a rival—ah, how great the punishments she will seek,
that I may not be able to bear children! This son made
my womb a thing to fear. What regions shall Alcmena seek?
What place, what region, what tract of the world
will defend me, or into what hiding-places shall I, a mother, be driven,
known everywhere through you? Shall I thus seek my homeland
and my wretched home? Eurystheus holds Argos;
shall I seek the wedded kingdom of Thebes and Ismenus
and my chamber, in which once I saw Jove,
beloved? O too happy, too happy,
if I myself had felt the lightning-wielding Jove!
Would that Alcides, an infant, had been cut
from my flesh! Now time is given: it is given
to see my son contending in glory with Jove,
that this too might be granted, to know what fate could
snatch from me. What people lives mindful of you,
O son? Now all the race is ungrateful.
Shall I seek Cleonae? Shall I seek the Arcadian peoples
and seek out the lands famed for your deeds?
Here the dire serpent fell, here the winged beast,
here the bloody king, here, broken by your hand,
the lion that, you buried, possesses the heaven:
if the land is grateful, let all the people defend
your Alcmena. Shall I seek the Thracian nations
and the peoples of the Hebrus? This land too, by your deserts,
is defended: the stables with their kingdom lie low.
Here peace was given, the bloody king laid low:
for where was it denied? What tomb shall I, an unhappy old woman,
seek for you? Over your pyre let the whole
world contend; what people, or what temples, what nations
ask for the relics of great Hercules?
Who, who seeks, who demands the burden of Alcmena?
What tombs, son, what mound is enough for you?
This whole world will be the title of your fame.
Why, my soul, do you tremble? You hold the ashes of Hercules;
embrace the bones: the relics will give aid,
they will be safeguard enough, they will terrify
kings, even your shade.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
The tears owed indeed
to your son restrain, mother of Alcides clothed in glory,
he is not to be mourned nor pressed with heavy prayer,
whoever by valor has taken his road from the fates:
eternal valor forbids Hercules to die.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text: Shall I quiet my complaints, a parent, my avenger lost?

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Earth and sea, and where the purple day
beholds either Ocean with its bright wheel—

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
How many sons, wretched, did I bury, a parent, in one?
I lacked a kingdom, but kingdoms I could give.
Alone among all the lands that mothers bear,
I spared my vows; nothing did I ask of the gods above
while my son was safe: what could the ardor of Hercules
not give me? What god could deny me
anything? My vows were in this hand:
whatever Jupiter denied, Hercules would give.
What such thing did any mortal mother bear?
Some mother stiffened, when, cut down in her whole
offspring, she stood, and twice seven, a flock,
one woman bewailed: to flocks could my son
be matched, how many he was worth? To wretched mothers still
a vast example was lacking: Alcmena I will give.
Cease, you mothers, if stubborn grief
still bids any to mourn, whom heavy sorrow
has turned to stone; yield, all of you, to these evils.
Come now, aged breast, O wretched hands,
beat yourselves, but a single aged old woman, worn out,
is enough for so great a funeral, which soon the whole
world will seek? Yet make ready for lamentation,
though wearied, your arms: that you may make for the gods
envy by your mourning, summon the race to lamentation.
Go, mourn the son of Alcmena
and great Jove,
for whom, when conceived, one day perished
and Dawn brought two nights together:
she herself perishes more than the light.
Mourn together, all you nations,
whose savage tyrants he bade
penetrate the Stygian homes
and, drenched with the peoples' blood, lay down the sword.
Render the weeping owed to deserts so great,
let the whole, the whole world resound:
let dark-blue Crete weep for Alcides,
land dear to the great Thunderer:
let a hundred peoples beat their arms;
now Curetes, now Corybantes,
shake the Idaean arms with your hands:
with arms it is fitting to mourn him;
now, now bewail a true funeral:
Alcides lies low,
not less, Crete, than the Thunderer himself.
Weep, Arcadians, for the death of Hercules,
a race born before Phoebe arose:
let the ridges of Parthenius and Pheneus resound
and let heavy lamentation strike Maenalus.
A groan for great Alcides demands
the bristling boar laid low in your fields
and the bird bidden to follow his arrows,
its plumage veiling the whole day.
Weep, Argive Cleonae, weep:
here the lion that once terrified
your walls
my son's right hand broke:
give blows, Bistonian mothers,
and let cold Hebrus resound with lamentations:
weep for Alcides,
because no infant is born in the stables
nor do herds tear your flesh;
let the land freed from Antaeus weep
and the tract snatched from wild Geryon:
mourn with me, wretched nations,
let either Tethys hear the blows,
you too, hastening throng of the world,
weep, you powers, for the fortunes of Hercules:
your world, you gods above, my Alcides
bore upon his neck, and the heaven,
when the bearer of the star-bearing Olympus,
Atlas, freed of his weight, breathed again:
where now are your citadels, Jupiter?
Where the palace of the promised world?
Surely Alcides, a mortal, dies,
surely is buried. How often your weapons
and your torches he spared,
how often the fire was to be scattered!
Against me at least hurl your torch
and think me Semele.
Now, O son, have you the Elysian homes,
now do you hold the shore
to which nature calls the peoples?
Or, after the hound was snatched, did black Styx
bar your road, and on the very threshold
of Dis do the fates delay you?
What tumult now, O son, holds the shades
and the ghosts?
Has the ferryman fled, his bark drawn away,
and, the Thessalian Centaurs stirred,
does the hoof strike the astonished ghosts,
and has the hydra, terrified, plunged
its snakes beneath the waters,
and do your labors, O son, fear you?
I am deceived, deceived, raving in my frenzy.
Neither do the ghosts and shades fear you.
No tawny hide, snatched from the Argive
lion, covered with its mane,
clothes your left arm, dire,
and no beast's teeth wall round your temples:
the gift of your quiver has passed away
and your weaker right hand will now send no shafts;
unarmed you go, O son, through the shades,
among which you will dwell forever.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Why, while I hold the kingdoms of the starry pole
and am at last given back to heaven, do you bid me
feel my fate by your lamentation? Spare me: now my valor
has made a road for me to the stars and to the very gods above.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Whence, whence does a sound strike my trembling
ears? Whence does a crash check my tears?
I recognize that chaos has been conquered.
From the Styx, O son, do you return again to me,
and has dire death been broken more than once?
Have you conquered again the regions of death,
the bark and the sad fords of the underworld?
Is languid Acheron now passable,
and is it permitted to you alone to return,
nor do the fates hold you after your funeral?
Or has Pluto barred your road
and, fearful, dreaded for his kingdom?
Surely I saw you set upon the blazing
woods, when most of all
the dread of the flame raged toward heaven:
you burned. Why did the farthest regions
not hold, why, your shade?
What did your ghosts fear, I pray?
Are you, even as a shade, too dreadful for Dis?

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
The pools of groaning Cocytus do not hold me,
nor has the dark bark borne my shade across;
spare now, mother, your complaints: the ghosts but once
and the shades I saw; whatever in me of you
was mortal, the conquering fire has taken away:
my father's part is given to heaven, your part to the flames.
Therefore lay aside the lamentation that an idle mother
prepares for her son; let mourning go to base things:
valor strains to the stars, fear to death.
Present from the stars, mother, I, Alcides, proclaim:
punishment soon bloody Eurystheus shall pay you;
borne in a car, you shall pass over his proud head.
Now it befits me to enter the heavenly tract:
again has Alcides conquered the infernal regions.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Wait a little while—he is gone, from my eyes he departs,
to the stars he is borne. Am I deceived, or does my mind think
it has seen my son? My wretched mind is unbelieving.
You are a god, and the world holds you forever.
I believe your triumphs; I will seek the kingdom of Thebes
and sing of a new divinity added to the temples.

title: Hercules Oetaeus
text:
Never is glorious valor borne
to the Stygian shades: the brave live on,
nor through the Lethaean streams shall savage
fate drag you, but when, the day consumed,
it shall demand the final hours,
glory will open the road to the gods above.
But you, great tamer of beasts
and at once the pacifier of the world, be present;
now too look back upon our lands,
and if any monster with new face
shall shake the peoples with heavy terror,
do you break it with the three-forked lightnings:
braver than your own father,
hurl the bolts.
